title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
The Fellegi-Sunter model estimates the probability structure of agreement patterns for true matches and non-matches, using quantities such as the m- and u-probabilities to construct a likelihood-based match score. Unlike the workshop’s fixed weighted score, it estimates linkage uncertainty from the data rather than assigning similarity weights only by rule.



Records with a reliable unique identifier can be linked directly because the identifier unambiguously determines whether two records belong to the same entity. Records without such an identifier require probabilistic linkage because names and other identifying fields may contain missing values, spelling errors, or measurement error, making the match uncertain.

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Data-Generating Process
The workshop simulates two administrative files, TRS and TEA, with 500 records each. The first 100 TEA records are generated as true matches to the first 100 TRS records. The baseline simulation corrupts 20% of those true matches by changing a first name, introducing a last-name typo, or shifting a date of birth by one day. I retained set.seed(42) for reproducibility.

Corruption-Rate Sensitivity


Show code
run_corruption_test <- function(rate) {

  set.seed(42)

  trs <- create_trs_data(500)
  tea <- create_tea_data(
    trs,
    n = 500,
    num_matches = 100,
    corruption_rate = rate
  )

  validation <- create_validation_set(trs, tea)

  trs_c <- trs %>%
    mutate(
      first_name_std = standardize_names(first_name),
      last_name_std = standardize_names(last_name),
      first_initial = substr(first_name_std, 1, 1),
      dob_std = standardize_date(dob)
    )

  tea_c <- tea %>%
    mutate(
      first_name_std = standardize_names(first_name),
      last_name_std = standardize_names(last_name),
      first_initial = substr(first_name_std, 1, 1),
      dob_std = standardize_date(dob)
    )

  det <- deterministic_linkage(trs_c, tea_c)

  ua <- det$remaining_a
  ub <- det$remaining_b

  last_sim <- calculate_similarity_efficient(
    ua$last_name_std, ub$last_name_std
  )

  first_sim <- calculate_similarity_efficient(
    ua$first_name_std, ub$first_name_std
  )

  dob_sim2 <- outer(
    as.numeric(ua$dob_std),
    as.numeric(ub$dob_std),
    function(x, y) {
      d <- abs(x - y)
      ifelse(d == 0, 1, ifelse(d == 1, 0.95, 0))
    }
  )

  comparisons <- expand_grid(
    idx_a = 1:nrow(ua),
    idx_b = 1:nrow(ub)
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      record_id_a = ua$record_id[idx_a],
      record_id_b = ub$record_id[idx_b],
      last_name_sim = sapply(
        1:n(),
        function(k) last_sim[idx_a[k], idx_b[k]]
      ),
      first_name_sim = sapply(
        1:n(),
        function(k) first_sim[idx_a[k], idx_b[k]]
      ),
      dob_sim = sapply(
        1:n(),
        function(k) dob_sim2[idx_a[k], idx_b[k]]
      ),
      match_score =
        0.40 * last_name_sim +
        0.30 * first_name_sim +
        0.30 * dob_sim
    )

  prob_links <- comparisons %>%
    filter(match_score > 0.95)

  combined <- bind_rows(
    det$matches %>%
      transmute(
        trs_record_id = record_id_a,
        tea_record_id = record_id_b,
        match_score = 0.99
      ),
    prob_links %>%
      transmute(
        trs_record_id = record_id_a,
        tea_record_id = record_id_b,
        match_score = match_score
      )
  )

  quality <- assess_linkage_quality(combined, validation)

  tibble(
    corruption_rate = rate,
    rule1 = det$summary$Matches[1],
    rule2 = det$summary$Matches[2],
    rule3 = det$summary$Matches[3],
    probabilistic = nrow(prob_links),
    precision = quality$metrics$Value[
      quality$metrics$Metric == "Precision"
    ],
    recall = quality$metrics$Value[
      quality$metrics$Metric == "Recall"
    ],
    f1 = quality$metrics$Value[
      quality$metrics$Metric == "F1-Score"
    ]
  )
}

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Answer-Key Sensitivity
The workshop sensitivity function evaluates only the probabilistic candidate pairs even though most true matches have already been recovered by deterministic rules. I therefore compared the original sensitivity results with a complete evaluation that retains deterministic matches and evaluates decisions against the complete 500 × 500 pair universe. Because the supplied validation set contains only the 100 known positive matches, I expanded the evaluation to all 500 × 500 possible record pairs and treated every pair not listed in the validation set as a non-match.


Show code
sensitivity_old <- sensitivity_results

sensitivity_analysis_complete <- function(
    all_comparisons,
    det_result,
    validation_set) {

  thresholds <- seq(0.70, 0.99, by = 0.05)
  results <- tibble()

  for (threshold in thresholds) {

    prob_matches <- all_comparisons %>%
      filter(match_score >= threshold) %>%
      transmute(
        trs_record_id = record_id_a,
        tea_record_id = record_id_b
      )

    det_matches <- det_result$matches %>%
      transmute(
        trs_record_id = record_id_a,
        tea_record_id = record_id_b
      )

    test_matches <- bind_rows(
      det_matches,
      prob_matches
    ) %>%
      distinct()

    answer_key <- expand_grid(
      trs_record_id = trs_data$record_id,
      tea_record_id = tea_data$record_id
    ) %>%
      mutate(
        true_match = if_else(
          paste(trs_record_id, tea_record_id) %in%
            paste(
              validation_set$trs_record_id,
              validation_set$tea_record_id
            ),
          1L, 0L
        )
      ) %>%
      left_join(
        test_matches %>% mutate(our_match = 1L),
        by = c("trs_record_id", "tea_record_id")
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        our_match = replace_na(our_match, 0L)
      )

    tp <- sum(
      answer_key$true_match == 1 &
        answer_key$our_match == 1
    )
    fp <- sum(
      answer_key$true_match == 0 &
        answer_key$our_match == 1
    )
    fn <- sum(
      answer_key$true_match == 1 &
        answer_key$our_match == 0
    )

    precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else 0
    recall <- if (tp + fn > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else 0
    f1 <- if (precision + recall > 0) {
      2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
    } else {
      0
    }

    results <- bind_rows(
      results,
      tibble(
        threshold = threshold,
        num_matches = nrow(test_matches),
        precision = precision,
        recall = recall,
        f1 = f1
      )
    )
  }

  results
}

text:
Blocking
I blocked candidate pairs on the first letter of the standardized last name.


Show code
pairs_before <- nrow(all_comparisons)

ua_block <- unmatched_a %>%
  mutate(
    block_letter = substr(last_name_std, 1, 1)
  ) %>%
  select(
    record_id_a = record_id,
    first_name_std_a = first_name_std,
    last_name_std_a = last_name_std,
    dob_std_a = dob_std,
    block_letter
  )

ub_block <- unmatched_b %>%
  mutate(
    block_letter = substr(last_name_std, 1, 1)
  ) %>%
  select(
    record_id_b = record_id,
    first_name_std_b = first_name_std,
    last_name_std_b = last_name_std,
    dob_std_b = dob_std,
    block_letter
  )

blocked_comparisons <- ua_block %>%
  inner_join(
    ub_block,
    by = "block_letter",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    last_name_sim =
      1 - stringdist(
        last_name_std_a,
        last_name_std_b,
        method = "jw"
      ),
    first_name_sim =
      1 - stringdist(
        first_name_std_a,
        first_name_std_b,
        method = "jw"
      ),
    dob_diff =
      abs(as.numeric(dob_std_a - dob_std_b)),
    dob_sim = case_when(
      dob_diff == 0 ~ 1,
      dob_diff == 1 ~ 0.95,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    match_score =
      0.40 * last_name_sim +
      0.30 * first_name_sim +
      0.30 * dob_sim
  )

pairs_after <- nrow(blocked_comparisons)

remaining_true_matches <- validation_set %>%
  semi_join(
    unmatched_a,
    by = c("trs_record_id" = "record_id")
  ) %>%
  semi_join(
    unmatched_b,
    by = c("tea_record_id" = "record_id")
  )

reachable_true_matches <- blocked_comparisons %>%
  select(
    trs_record_id = record_id_a,
    tea_record_id = record_id_b
  ) %>%
  semi_join(
    remaining_true_matches,
    by = c("trs_record_id", "tea_record_id")
  )

    pairs_before,

    round(100 * (1 - pairs_after / pairs_before), 2),
    nrow(remaining_true_matches),
    nrow(reachable_true_matches),
    nrow(remaining_true_matches) -

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Data-Based Weights
The workshop used fixed weights of 0.40 for last name, 0.30 for first name, and 0.30 for date of birth. I instead estimated agreement probabilities from the full pair universe. Because zero agreement probabilities would make log(m/u) infinite, I used Jeffreys smoothing (+0.5) before calculating the log ratios.


Show code
weight_pairs_full <- expand_grid(
  idx_a = 1:nrow(trs_clean),
  idx_b = 1:nrow(tea_clean)
) %>%
  mutate(
    record_id_a = trs_clean$record_id[idx_a],
    record_id_b = tea_clean$record_id[idx_b],
    last_agree = as.integer(
      trs_clean$last_name_std[idx_a] ==
        tea_clean$last_name_std[idx_b]
    ),
    first_agree = as.integer(
      trs_clean$first_name_std[idx_a] ==
        tea_clean$first_name_std[idx_b]
    ),
    dob_agree = as.integer(
      trs_clean$dob_std[idx_a] ==
        tea_clean$dob_std[idx_b]
    ),
    is_true_match =
      paste(record_id_a, record_id_b) %in%
      paste(
        validation_set$trs_record_id,
        validation_set$tea_record_id
      )
  )

estimate_mu <- function(x, true_match) {

  x_true <- x[true_match]
  x_false <- x[!true_match]

  m <- (sum(x_true) + 0.5) /
    (length(x_true) + 1)

  u <- (sum(x_false) + 0.5) /
    (length(x_false) + 1)

  c(m = m, u = u)
}

mu_last <- estimate_mu(
  weight_pairs_full$last_agree,
  weight_pairs_full$is_true_match
)

mu_first <- estimate_mu(
  weight_pairs_full$first_agree,
  weight_pairs_full$is_true_match
)

mu_dob <- estimate_mu(
  weight_pairs_full$dob_agree,
  weight_pairs_full$is_true_match
)

mu_table_full <- tibble(
  field = c("Last name", "First name", "DOB"),
  m = c(mu_last["m"], mu_first["m"], mu_dob["m"]),
  u = c(mu_last["u"], mu_first["u"], mu_dob["u"])
) %>%
  mutate(
    log_m_u = log(m / u),
    weight = log_m_u / sum(log_m_u)
  )

The raw agreement weights were the field-specific log(m/u) values. I normalized the three positive log(m/u) values to sum to one so that the final weighted similarity score remained on the 0–1 scale while preserving the relative contribution of each field. Threshold Calibration
I evaluated thresholds from 0.70 to 0.99 in increments of 0.01 using the blocked, data-weighted candidate scores while retaining the deterministic matches.


Show code

  seq(0.70, 0.99, by = 0.01),
  function(threshold) {

    prob_links <- weighted_comparisons %>%
      filter(data_based_score >= threshold) %>%
      transmute(
        trs_record_id = record_id_a,
        tea_record_id = record_id_b
      )

    test_matches <- bind_rows(
      det_result$matches %>%
        transmute(
          trs_record_id = record_id_a,
          tea_record_id = record_id_b
        ),
      prob_links
    ) %>%
      distinct()

    quality <- assess_linkage_quality(
      test_matches,
      validation_set
    )

    tibble(
      threshold = threshold,
      num_matches = nrow(test_matches),
      precision = quality$metrics$Value[
        quality$metrics$Metric == "Precision"
      ],
      recall = quality$metrics$Value[
        quality$metrics$Metric == "Recall"
      ],
      f1 = quality$metrics$Value[
        quality$metrics$Metric == "F1-Score"

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Review Band
I defined the manual-review band as scores from 0.85 up to, but not including, the selected 0.89 automatic-link threshold. I retained 0.85 as the lower bound for comparability with the workshop and used 0.89 as the upper bound because pairs at or above 0.89 were automatically linked; pairs below 0.85 were treated as having insufficient evidence to justify manual review.


Show code

review_band <- weighted_comparisons %>%
  filter(
    data_based_score >= 0.85,
    data_based_score < chosen_threshold

  mutate(
    is_true_match =
      paste(record_id_a, record_id_b) %in%
      paste(
        validation_set$trs_record_id,
        validation_set$tea_record_id

Therefore, the requested ten false-positive and ten false-negative cases do not exist at the chosen threshold. I do not fabricate cases that are absent from the simulated results. To show what kinds of errors the score can produce when the decision threshold changes, I provide a supplementary diagnostic using a lower threshold (0.70) for false positives and a higher threshold (0.99) for false negatives. These supplementary cases are not errors from the chosen 0.89 threshold.

true_pair_key <- paste(
  validation_set$trs_record_id,
  validation_set$tea_record_id
)

make_diagnostic_set <- function(threshold) {

  prob_links <- weighted_comparisons %>%
    filter(data_based_score >= threshold) %>%
    transmute(
      trs_record_id = record_id_a,
      tea_record_id = record_id_b,
      match_score = data_based_score,
      last_name_sim,
      first_name_sim,
      dob_sim
    )

  det_links <- det_result$matches %>%
    transmute(

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Report
This analysis asks a simple administrative-data question: how many people appear in both the simulated TRS and TEA files, and how confidently can the two records be treated as belonging to the same person? The files contain 500 records each, and the simulation provides a known answer key with 100 true cross-file matches. That answer key makes direct evaluation possible, although such certainty would rarely exist in a real administrative-data project.
I began with the workshop’s deterministic rules. The strictest rule required exact agreement on last name, first name, and date of birth. Two additional rules allowed a first initial or a one-day difference in date of birth. Under the baseline 20% corruption setting, the deterministic rules recovered 93 of the 100 true matches with no false positives. The probabilistic stage then evaluated the remaining records using partial similarity on last name, first name, and date of birth. The probabilistic step recovered the seven remaining true matches and added no false matches under the final specification.
Changing the data-generating process showed how linkage performance depends on data quality. At 10% corruption, recall was 0.99 and F1 was 0.995. At 40% corruption, recall fell to 0.93 and F1 to 0.964, while precision remained 1.00. Exact Rule 1 matches dropped from 90 to 60 as corruption increased. The largest practical effect of noisier identifiers in this simulation was therefore a loss of recall: true matches became harder to recover, even though the algorithm continued to avoid incorrect links.
I also corrected the workshop sensitivity evaluation. The supplied validation set contains the 100 known positive matches, while the workshop shortcut evaluates only the probabilistic candidate pairs after deterministic matches have been removed. I therefore expanded the evaluation to the full 500 × 500 pair universe, treating all pairs not listed in the validation set as non-matches. When deterministic and probabilistic decisions were evaluated together, recall increased by 0.93 at each tested workshop threshold. This matters because an evaluation that ignores records already linked deterministically can make a successful linkage procedure appear to have very low recall.
Blocking on the first letter of standardized last name reduced the probabilistic candidate set from 165,649 pairs to 19,030, an 88.51% reduction. All seven true matches entering the probabilistic stage remained reachable, so this blocking rule improved computational efficiency without lowering recall in this simulation. However, blocking is still a substantive restriction: if a true pair had different first letters after corruption or standardization, it would become impossible to recover regardless of its later similarity score.
I replaced the workshop’s fixed 0.40/0.30/0.30 weights with weights based on estimated agreement probabilities. After Jeffreys smoothing, the raw log(m/u) values were normalized to sum to one so that the weighted score stayed on the 0–1 scale. The resulting weights were approximately 0.176 for last name, 0.181 for first name, and 0.644 for date of birth. DOB received the greatest weight because exact DOB agreement was common among true matches but extremely rare among non-matches.
Using these weights, I evaluated thresholds from 0.70 to 0.99. The first threshold that achieved precision = 1.00, recall = 1.00, and F1 = 1.00 was 0.89, so I selected 0.89 as the final automatic-link threshold. I prioritized F1 because both error types matter for the study question. A false positive joins records from different people and can inflate the estimated overlap or attach one person’s information to another. A false negative omits a person who truly appears in both systems and biases the overlap count downward. The review band was set from 0.85 to below 0.89; it contained two pairs, and neither was a true match.
At the chosen threshold, the final linkage produced 100 true positives, 0 false positives, and 0 false negatives, so the estimated TRS–TEA overlap is exactly 100 in this simulation. The absence of errors at the chosen threshold also means that the assignment’s request for ten false positives and ten false negatives cannot literally be satisfied without inventing cases. I therefore report that none exist at 0.89 and use alternative thresholds only as supplementary diagnostics to illustrate the types of errors that would occur if the policy were made more permissive or more restrictive.
The perfect final score should not be generalized to real administrative data. The same simulated answer key was used to estimate data-based weights, choose the threshold, and evaluate final performance, so the result is optimistic. If the answer key itself contained mistakes, then the estimated m and u probabilities, field weights, threshold curve, and reported precision and recall could all shift. Conclusions would remain credible only if the key correctly identified the true cross-file matches and if pairs not listed in the key were truly non-matches. Real files can also contain missing identifiers, multiple errors in the same record, duplicate people, name changes, and demographic groups with systematically different rates of common names or data-entry error. Those groups could be linked less reliably and could therefore be over- or under-represented in downstream counts. A linked file should therefore be treated as a documented claim about identity, not as error-free ground truth.

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Data Note
The data are simulated administrative records generated by record_linkage_workshop.R with set.seed(42). The analysis uses TRS and TEA files with 500 records each and evaluates corruption rates of 0.10, 0.20, and 0.40. The final method combines three deterministic rules, blocking on the first letter of standardized last name, data-based field weights, and an automatic-link threshold of 0.89. The known answer key contains 100 simulated true matches.
The simulation simplifies several features of real administrative data. Names are drawn from small predefined lists, corruption is introduced only among true matched records, and each selected record receives one of three simple changes: a first-name abbreviation, a last-name typo, or a one-day DOB shift. It therefore leaves out missing identifiers, simultaneous errors across several fields, name changes, duplicate individuals, and many other sources of linkage uncertainty. The answer key also assumes that the 100 designated pairs are correct and that all other cross-file pairs are non-matches. If those assumptions were wrong, the estimated weights, threshold performance, and final quality metrics would also be wrong. No generated individual-level records are posted separately.

When Is Scraping the Right Tool?
Web scraping is appropriate when the information needed for research is publicly available on a website but is not available through a structured API, downloadable dataset, or other reliable machine-readable source. When an official API or structured dataset exists, it is generally preferable because its schema and data-generation process are more stable and reproducible than scraping a changing webpage.

4. Data Plan

Web Data Acquisition Plan
For my research, I am interested in crime analysis, policing, public safety, environmental criminology, crime mapping, and GIS. One potential source is the City of Dallas Open Data and Police Public Data system, which provides public access to police offense and incident information. I would prefer this official source because the data are published by the City of Dallas and Dallas Police Department and are more appropriate for analyzing local crime patterns and locations than a third-party website.
Before collecting data, I would check the applicable robots.txt file for the specific endpoint and comply with any restrictions it specifies. The City of Dallas makes public data available for exploration and analysis through its Open Data system, while its general website disclaimer restricts commercial use without written permission. The City also provides structured access through GIS REST services, including police geographic layers that support formats such as JSON and GeoJSON and pagination. Therefore, when the necessary variables are available through an API, REST service, or downloadable dataset, I would use those structured sources rather than scrape webpages directly. Web scraping would only be used when relevant public information is available on a webpage but not through a structured alternative.
For a project examining crime patterns and neighborhood change, I would collect incident-level crime records over multiple years and connect them to geographic units such as police beats, census tracts, or neighborhoods. I would limit requests to the variables and time periods needed, use pagination and reasonable request intervals when necessary, and cache the raw data locally to avoid repeated requests to the server.
Because web-based data systems can change over time, I would monitor field names, record counts, missing values, date ranges, and sample observations after collection. I would also preserve the original raw data and record the collection date so that changes in the source can be documented and the data-production process can be reproduced.

title: Assignment 6: Text Analytics with quanteda
text:
The first corpus is an archived set of tweets collected during the November 2021 Biden–Xi summit. Because the API access that produced this dataset is no longer available in the same form, the corpus can be analyzed but cannot simply be recollected today. Its interpretation therefore depends on the original keyword strategy and collection window rather than representing all public opinion about the summit.
The archived corpus contains 14,520 tweets collected around the 2021 Biden–Xi summit.











The most frequent vocabulary is dominated by the two presidents, the summit itself, China, and terms connected with the virtual meeting. This provides a simple overview of what was most visible in the collected discussion, although frequency alone does not indicate whether a term was used positively or negatively.












The hashtag network shows clusters of terms that appeared together. Central hashtags such as those referring to Biden, China, and Xi connect the summit to broader political and human-rights discussions.












Unlike the hashtag network, the mention network is more fragmented. This indicates that frequently mentioned accounts did not form one single communication cluster in the archived dataset.












The LSA representation summarizes similarities in word use across thousands of tweets. The visible clusters suggest recurring patterns of language, although the latent dimensions themselves do not have an automatic substantive interpretation.
Overall, the tweet corpus captures immediate public communication around the summit. It should not be treated as a representative sample of U.S. or global public opinion because the original query and collection period determined which tweets entered the dataset, participation on Twitter/X is selective, and highly active users can contribute disproportionately.

text: Anscombe’s four datasets may have similar statistical results, but the actual data patterns identified by graphs are very different. The first dataset shows a relatively normal linear relationship, but the second dataset shows a curved pattern. So, a simple linear regression line does not fully explain the data pattern. In the third dataset, most of the points show a consistent pattern, but one outlier strongly influences the result. Lastly, in the fourth dataset, most points are concentrated in one location, but one point strongly impacts the result. Anscombe’s four datasets show that it is difficult to fully understand the actual data pattern by just checking the mean, correlation, and regression results. Therefore, when we analyze data, it is suggested to draw graphs first and check the patterns and outliers instead of just checking the statistical results.

3. Crime Rate Chart Critique

This graph shows the trend in Index crime in the United States from 2014 to 2024, and it is good to see the changes in the overall crime rate by separating violent crime and property crime. Also, it has a good point that the graph clearly indicates that the 2021 data are not comparable with other years. However, there is also a critical point: the 2024 data are not final annual data but preliminary data estimated based on the percent change between 2023 and early 2024, but they are described in almost the same way as other years’ final data. In other words, readers can misunderstand that the 2024 data are also final data like other years. Also, the title indicates that the crime rate in 2024 is the lowest since 1961, but the graph only shows crime rates from 2014 to 2024, so the readers cannot check the long-term comparison themselves through the graph. Lastly, the total height of the bar already shows the total Index crime, but showing the same value again with a line may be redundant. Therefore, the 2024 estimated numbers should be clearly distinguished using a different color or separate annotation. Also, to support the title of long-term comparison, data from a longer time period should be presented to increase the accuracy and clarity of the graph.
Source: Prison Policy Initiative, “U.S. crime rates continue to fall, and preliminary data indicate that the 2024 crime rate was the lowest since 1961”

Chart 1: Variable-Width Column
The 2025 HPI data were summarized by continent. The width of each column represents total population, while the height represents mean HPI across countries within each continent.

hpi_continent <- hpi_2025 %>%
  group_by(Continent) %>%
  summarise(
    population = sum(Population, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_hpi = mean(HPI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    continent_name = case_when(
      Continent == 1 ~ "Latin America",
      Continent == 2 ~ "N America & Oceania",
      Continent == 3 ~ "Western Europe",
      Continent == 4 ~ "Middle East & N. Africa",
      Continent == 5 ~ "Africa",
      Continent == 6 ~ "South Asia",
      Continent == 7 ~ "Eastern Europe & Central Asia",
      Continent == 8 ~ "East Asia"
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_hpi)) %>%
  mutate(
    xmax = cumsum(population),
    xmin = lag(xmax, default = 0),
    xmid = (xmin + xmax) / 2,
    continent_name = factor(
      continent_name,
      levels = continent_name
    )
  )


ggplot(hpi_continent) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = xmin,
      xmax = xmax,
      ymin = 0,
      ymax = mean_hpi,
      fill = continent_name
    ),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +

  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = xmid,
      y = mean_hpi + 1.2,
      label = sprintf("%.1f", mean_hpi)

400% Zoom Comparison
I opened each exported file and compared the text and lines at 400% zoom.
PDF: The text and lines remained sharp and clear at 400% zoom.
SVG: The text and lines also remained sharp and clear at 400% zoom.
PNG: The image remained fairly clear, but some pixelation was visible around the text and lines at 400% zoom.
JPG: The text and lines appeared less sharp, with more noticeable pixelation at 400% zoom.
TIFF: The image quality remained high, but some pixelation was visible at 400% zoom because it is a raster format.
BMP: The text and lines also became pixelated at 400% zoom, although there were no noticeable compression artifacts.


Recommended Formats
For a journal article, I would use PDF because it is a vector format and remains sharp when resized.
For a web page, I would use SVG because it remains sharp at different screen sizes and works well for simple graphics.
For a PowerPoint slide, I would use PNG because it is widely supported and provides good image quality.

title: Assignment 5
text:
Reflection
Pie charts can be useful when there are only a few categories and the purpose is to show simple parts of a whole. Cleveland and McGill (1984) show that people compare positions and lengths more accurately than angles and areas. Because pie charts rely on angles and areas, they are not ideal when categories have similar values.
In my pie chart, there are only three cylinder categories, so the general differences are easy to see. However, the bar chart allows more precise comparison among the categories. Therefore, I would use a pie chart only when the number of categories is small and exact comparisons are not the main purpose.

How does economic wealth relate to sustainable wellbeing across countries?

Overparameterization is the situation of using too many variables or candidate predictors compared to the number of observations. The two concepts are related, and the risk of overfitting can increase as more candidates are considered.
GFT compared 50 million search terms to 1,152 CDC observations. Among these candidates, if we select search terms that show high correlations, variables that show spurious patterns by chance can be included even though they are not directly related to actual influenza. In fact, a search term that was not directly related to influenza, such as “high school basketball,” showed a high correlation (Lazer et al., 2014).

It is important to validate whether performance is maintained in new data. GFT shows that larger amounts of data or more variables do not always mean better prediction. Code
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(patchwork)

# Dashboard data created for Assignment 8
dashboard_data <- read_csv(
  "subway_arrests_dashboard_2024.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Create one row per station for 2024
station_summary <- dashboard_data |>
  group_by(
    station_complex_id,
    station_complex,
    borough,
    latitude,
    longitude
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_ridership = sum(monthly_ridership, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_arrests = sum(arrest_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    arrests_per_100k =
      total_arrests / total_ridership * 100000,

    borough_name = case_when(
      borough %in% c("M", "Manhattan") ~ "Manhattan",
      borough %in% c("Bk", "Brooklyn") ~ "Brooklyn",
      borough %in% c("Q", "Queens") ~ "Queens",
      borough %in% c("Bx", "Bronx") ~ "Bronx",
      borough %in% c("SI", "Staten Island") ~ "Staten Island",
      TRUE ~ borough
    )
  )

# Summarize station measures by borough
borough_summary <- station_summary |>
  group_by(borough_name) |>
  summarise(
    total_ridership = sum(total_ridership, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_arrests = sum(total_arrests, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    arrests_per_100k =
      total_arrests / total_ridership * 100000
  )

# NYC Open Data Borough Boundaries
boroughs <- st_read(
  "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/gthc-hcne.geojson?$limit=5000",
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  transmute(
    borough_name = boroname,
    geometry
  )

# Join the project data to borough boundaries
borough_map <- boroughs |>
  left_join(
    borough_summary,
    by = "borough_name"
  )

# Station locations as spatial points
station_sf <- st_as_sf(
  station_summary,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
)

title: November 17 Colloquium: Silicon Sampling Methods in Public Opinion Research
text:
Reflection
I attended Lisa Argyle’s talk on Silicon Sampling Methods in Public Opinion Research. The presentation discussed how large language models can be used to simulate human responses in public opinion research, as well as some of the limitations of using synthetic responses in place of actual survey data.
One point I found especially interesting was the difference between generating responses that seem plausible and generating responses that accurately reflect human opinion. The presentation showed that synthetic survey responses can sometimes reproduce the general ordering or direction of public opinion while still overestimating some issues and underestimating others. This suggests that an LLM response can look reasonable without necessarily matching what people would actually say.
The talk also showed how many different choices can affect LLM-generated results. These include the model’s training data, post-training and alignment, prompting, and even the order in which survey response options are presented. I was particularly interested in the discussion of alignment. Models are usually trained to be helpful, honest, and harmless, but this can sometimes make them less willing to produce negative or socially undesirable opinions. That can become a problem when the goal is to represent the full range of actual public opinion.
Another useful part of the presentation was the discussion of different approaches to silicon sampling. Some researchers focus on whether information about human attitudes is already contained in the model and can be recovered through better prompting or fine-tuning. Others treat LLMs more like imperfect respondents whose output may need to be adjusted or combined with human data. The presentation also discussed the connection between LLMs and agent-based modeling.
The part that stayed with me most was the idea that researchers should decide what counts as success before evaluating silicon sampling. A model may not predict the response of a particular individual very well but may still reproduce an overall population pattern. This made me think more carefully about whether the relevant target is an individual response, a subgroup pattern, or an aggregate outcome.
Overall, the presentation made me see both the potential and the limitations of silicon sampling. I think LLMs can be useful research tools, but their responses should not automatically be treated as substitutes for human data. The results depend heavily on how the model is trained and used, and researchers need to be clear about what they are trying to reproduce and how they will evaluate whether the model is doing it well enough.

title: Prepare for Class 5: Write and Post
text:
Google Flu Trends (GFT) was a system designed to rapidly estimate influenza outbreaks by using Google search data. In the early study, the frequency of search queries showed a high correlation with CDC influenza-like illness data, so it showed the possibility of estimating influenza activity one or two weeks earlier than official reports (Ginsberg et al., 2009). However, later GFT revealed a problem of largely overestimating actual influenza levels.
Lazer et al. (2014) argue that two of the causes were big data hubris and algorithm dynamics. Big data hubris is an overconfident attitude that assumes large amounts of data can replace traditional data collection and analysis. However, problems with measurement validity and reliability still remain even when there is a large amount of data (Lazer et al., 2014).
Algorithm dynamics means the phenomenon where the data-generating process itself changes as search algorithms and user behavior change over time. If search results or recommendation systems change, the way people search can also change, so it is difficult to assume that a model that worked well in the past will continuously show the same performance. Also, the core search terms and analytical process were not fully disclosed, so it was difficult for other researchers to accurately replicate the original analysis (Lazer et al., 2014).
Through this reading, I learned that a large amount of data alone does not guarantee better analysis, and that it is important to understand how data are generated and measured.

title: Prepare for Class 5: Write and Post
text:
Overfitting and Overparameterization
Overfitting is the phenomenon in which a model is excessively tailored to specific data rather than general patterns, leading to poor performance on new data. Overparameterization is the situation of using too many variables or candidate predictors compared to the number of observations. The two concepts are related, and the risk of overfitting can increase as more candidates are considered.
GFT compared 50 million search terms to 1,152 CDC observations. Among these candidates, if we select search terms that show high correlations, variables that show spurious patterns by chance can be included even though they are not directly related to actual influenza. In fact, a search term that was not directly related to influenza, such as “high school basketball,” showed a high correlation (Lazer et al., 2014).
Therefore, a model should not be judged as successful just because it shows high correlations and a good model fit in the training data. It is important to validate whether performance is maintained in new data. GFT shows that larger amounts of data or more variables do not always mean better prediction.

section: Wickham Talk: Data Visualization and Data Science
text:
Wickham Talk: Data Visualization and Data Science
In Wickham’s talk, many techniques and methods are introduced, such as the grammar of graphics, tidy data, tidyverse, ggplot2, data reshaping, faceting, animation, overplotting, functions and iterations, and reproducible reports. In particular, his discussion shows that if we organize data in a tidy structure and make visualizations based on the principles of the grammar of graphics, we can make the analysis process more consistent and reproducible.
Moreover, Wickham distinguishes between exploratory visualization and polished visualization. In the exploratory stage, identifying patterns or problems is important, and in the final visualization, it is important to communicate results clearly to others. I agree that visualization and modeling are not substitutes, but have a complementary relationship. Visualization can show patterns that a model may miss, and a model can more systematically summarize or validate relationships.
However, using good tools does not automatically create a good visualization. Interpretation can differ depending on the selection of variables, scales, colors, and coordinate systems. Therefore, it is still the researcher’s role to judge which visualization fits the research question and audience.

Data Notes

Books to Scrape

Source and date collected: Books to Scrape, collected October 7, 2026.
Permission: The target path was checked with robotstxt, and the site is intended as a scraping sandbox.
Method: Data were collected with a polite session using HTML/CSS selectors and a five-second crawl delay.
Cleaning: Prices were converted to numeric values, ratings to integers from 1 to 5, and stock status to logical values.
Known gaps: The scraper depends on the current HTML structure and CSS class names, so a website redesign could break the selectors.



Quotes to Scrape

Source and date collected: Quotes to Scrape, collected October 7, 2026.
Permission: The site is designed for web-scraping practice, and requests were limited to one per second.
Method: Quotes were collected from the site’s API and converted from JSON into a structured tibble; the JavaScript page was also tested with a live browser.
Cleaning: Nested author and tag information was converted into one row per quote with text, author name, author slug, and tags.
Known gaps: The process depends on the API endpoint and response structure remaining available and unchanged.



YouTube Data API

Source and date collected: YouTube Data API v3, collected October 7, 2026.
Permission: Access was made through a personal API key stored securely in .Renviron.
Method: The documented YouTube Data API was queried for the ten most popular videos in the United States.
Cleaning: Nested JSON fields were converted into a table containing video ID, title, channel, and view count.
Known gaps: The results represent only the ten most popular videos returned at the time of collection, and view counts can change over time.

This exercise examines a model of the Happy Planet Index using population and happy life years.


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(vroom)
library(janitor)
library(easystats)

hpi2016 <- vroom::vroom(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/datavisualizationinpractice/main/data/happyplanetindex.csv",
  .name_repair = janitor::make_clean_names,
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    gdp_pc = readr::parse_number(gdp_capita_ppp)
  )

m_hpi <- lm(
  happy_planet_index ~ log(population) + happy_life_years,
  data = hpi2016
)






Show code
check_model(m_hpi)









The diagnostic checks do not indicate major problems with heteroscedasticity, multicollinearity, influential observations, or residual normality. The linearity panel shows some curvature, so possible nonlinearity is the main feature worth noting.

Show code

The coefficient for happy life years is positive, approximately 0.28, with a 95% confidence interval of about 0.20 to 0.36.



The Happy Planet Index is constructed using wellbeing, life expectancy, inequality, and ecological footprint. Happy life years already combines wellbeing and life expectancy. Therefore, the model partly explains an index using a variable that contains some of the same information used to construct that index, which limits substantive interpretation.
